title: Surprise regulatory fine on bank reputation and stock value

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
Causal method: Short‐horizon event study  
Rationale:  • The “treatment” (surprise fine announcement) occurs at a known, sharp date for each bank.  
 • Market efficiency implies that any causal valuation effect should be impounded in stock prices immediately, so abnormal returns in a narrow window around the announcement identify the causal effect.  

Key identifying assumptions  
1. Market model validity – in the absence of the announcement, the conditional expectation of the stock’s return is E[ret | mkt_ret] = αᵢ + βᵢ·mkt_ret; therefore abnormal returns (AR) capture the shock.  
2. No confounding news in the (-1,+1) window – the fine announcement is the only price–relevant information.  
3. Trading‐day independence – AR across firms are independent, so the cross-sectional t-test is valid.

If the average cumulative abnormal return (CAR) is more negative than the mechanical wealth transfer (-fine_ratio), investors penalise reputational damage over and above the cash outflow.

## 2. R Code
```r
############################################
# Surprise‐fine event study implementation #
############################################

# 1. Load packages ------------------------------------------------------------
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(data.table)   # fast aggregation
  library(dplyr)        # piping
})

# 2. Read data ---------------------------------------------------------------
file_path <- "experiments/exp_b/data/s17_data.csv"
dt <- fread(file_path)

# 3. Define windows ----------------------------------------------------------
est_start <- -10; est_end <- -2          # estimation window
evt_start <-  -1; evt_end <-  1          # main event window
evt_start_rb <- -2; evt_end_rb <- 2      # robustness event window

# 4. Helper: function to get CAR for a single stock --------------------------
get_car <- function(df, est_st, est_ed, ev_st, ev_ed){
  # estimation data
  est <- df %>% filter(event_day >= est_st & event_day <= est_ed)
  # alpha_i = mean( r_i - beta_i * r_m )
  alpha_i <- mean(est$ret - est$beta * est$mkt_ret, na.rm = TRUE)
  
  # event data
  ev  <- df %>% filter(event_day >= ev_st & event_day <= ev_ed)
  exp_ret <- alpha_i + ev$beta * ev$mkt_ret
  ar <- ev$ret - exp_ret
  car <- sum(ar, na.rm = TRUE)
  return(car)
}

# 5. Compute CARs -------------------------------------------------------------
car_main <- dt %>% 
  group_by(stock_id) %>% 
  group_modify(~ tibble(CAR = get_car(.x, est_start, est_end,
                                      evt_start, evt_end))) %>% 
  ungroup()

car_rb <- dt %>% 
  group_by(stock_id) %>% 
  group_modify(~ tibble(CAR_rb = get_car(.x, est_start, est_end,
                                         evt_start_rb, evt_end_rb))) %>% 
  ungroup()

# 6. Merge fine ratios (assumed constant per stock) ---------------------------
fine <- dt %>% distinct(stock_id, fine_ratio)
res  <- car_main %>% 
        inner_join(car_rb,  by = "stock_id") %>% 
        inner_join(fine,    by = "stock_id") %>% 
        mutate(rep_effect = CAR + fine_ratio,      # reputational component
               rep_effect_rb = CAR_rb + fine_ratio)

# 7. Tests --------------------------------------------------------------------
t_main <- t.test(res$rep_effect, mu = 0, alternative = "less")
t_rb   <- t.test(res$rep_effect_rb, mu = 0, alternative = "less")

# 8. Cross-sectional regression CAR ~ fine_ratio ------------------------------
reg <- lm(CAR ~ fine_ratio, data = res)

# 9. Print results ------------------------------------------------------------
cat("-------------------------------------------------\n")
cat("Main event window (−1,+1):\n")
cat("Mean CAR                :", round(mean(res$CAR), 4), "\n")
cat("Mean fine ratio         :", round(mean(res$fine_ratio), 4), "\n")
cat("Mean reputational effect:", round(mean(res$rep_effect), 4), "\n")
cat("t-statistic (H0: =0, one-sided <0):", round(t_main$statistic, 3),
    " p-value:", round(t_main$p.value, 4), "\n\n")

cat("Robustness 1 – wider event window (−2,+2):\n")
cat("Mean reputational effect:", round(mean(res$rep_effect_rb), 4), "\n")
cat("t-statistic:", round(t_rb$statistic, 3),
    " p-value:", round(t_rb$p.value, 4), "\n\n")

cat("Robustness 2 – cross-sectional slope (should be <-1 if extra penalty):\n")
cat("CAR = a + b * fine_ratio   -->  b̂ =", round(coef(reg)["fine_ratio"], 3),
    " (se =", round(summary(reg)$coefficients["fine_ratio", "Std. Error"], 3), ")\n")
cat("R² =", round(summary(reg)$r.squared, 3), "\n")
cat("-------------------------------------------------\n")
```

The script  
• builds αᵢ from the −10…−2 estimation window,  
• computes CARs over (-1,+1) and (-2,+2),  
• tests whether CAR + fine_ratio < 0 (reputational loss), and  
• runs a cross-sectional regression as another robustness check.

## 3. Expected Findings
Theory and prior evidence (e.g. Karpoff et al., 2008) suggest that the stock-price loss typically exceeds the direct wealth transfer. I therefore expect:

• Average fine_ratio ≈ -0.4 % of market cap.  
• Average CAR over (-1,+1) ≈ -1.2 %.  
• Reputational effect ≈ -0.8 % (t-stat ≈ -3), statistically significant.  

The robustness window (-2,+2) should yield a slightly larger in magnitude repercussion (≈ -1 %), and the slope in CAR ~ fine_ratio should be around ‑1.5, implying each $1 of fine destroys ≈ $1.5–$2 in shareholder value.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Event study with CAR decomposition: financial cost vs. reputational component
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: CAR exceeds fine/mktcap ratio, confirming reputational damage beyond monetary penalty
_ground_truth.main_effect: CAR ≈ −3.5%; reputational component ≈ −1.5% above direct cost
